sections.heading: Start With the Parts of the House You Can't See
body: A cold floor in January. An upstairs that never cools off in August. A furnace that runs and runs and never quite catches up.

Most people blame the windows, because the windows are the part you can see. But heat leaves a house through whatever part of it has the least in the way, and that is more often the attic, the floor or a gap around a pipe.

That's why we look at the whole house, not just one part of it. We tell you where it's losing comfort and fix what's actually leaking, whether it turns out to be the attic, the floor, an air leak, the windows or the furnace.

sections.heading: Insulation
body: An attic that's too hot to climb into by July is a house that's paying to cool the roof. A floor that's cold under your feet usually has a crawl space under it with nothing between you and the ground.
Heat moves toward cold, so in winter your warmth heads up and out, and in summer the attic heat comes down. Insulation is what slows that down.

We insulate attics, floors, crawl spaces and exterior walls, and we wrap and insulate the underside of mobile homes. Before attic insulation goes down, our crews flag the electrical junction boxes so they can be found again. If a house has no way into the attic, we make one.

sections.heading: Air Sealing and Weatherization
body: Some drafts aren't about insulation at all. They come in around a back door, under a sink where the pipes go through the wall, at the fireplace, or at the duct work by a floor register.

Sealing those gaps is the other half of a weatherized house. We install door sweeps and weatherstripping, seal around plumbing, seal duct work at the registers, wrap pipes and put in smoke alarms, and we'll seal a fireplace if you ask.

A lot of this work happens through the weatherization program run by the South Central Kansas Economic Development District (SCKEDD). We work under that program, and the work is the same insulation and sealing.

sections.heading: Window Replacement
body: Windows wear out in ways you can feel before you can see them.
The curtains move with the window shut. The glass is cold to the touch. There's fog between the panes, a sash that won't stay up, or street noise that comes straight through.
Each one means a window that has stopped sealing, and you're heating and cooling the outdoors through it.
We replace them with vinyl windows, and our own crew puts them in.
Windows are built to the size of your openings, so there is a wait between the estimate and the install day. The install itself is a day's work.

sections.heading: Furnace and AC
body: A furnace that can't keep up is often fighting a house that leaks. Put a new one in a house with an empty attic and you've bought a bigger engine for a car with the windows down.

We install new furnaces and air conditioners, and we install Hitachi mini-split systems. Hitachi's own contractor page lists us as an authorized manufacturer's rep. Because we insulate too, the same company can fix the equipment and the house around it.

items.q: Should I replace my windows or add insulation first?
items.a: If the windows aren't fogged, broken or hard to use, and a room is still hot or cold, start with the attic and floor. They are the likelier cause, and it's usually the cheaper fix. We do both, so we can tell you which one your house needs.

items.q: How long does a job take?
items.a: Many insulation jobs are done in a day. A whole-house job can bring in more than one crew. Window installs take a day, but the windows are built to order first, so allow weeks between the estimate and install day.

items.q: Do you do weatherization program work?
items.a: Yes. We work under the SCKEDD Weatherization program. The program decides who qualifies and when your home comes up, and the wait can be long.
Our crews clean up before they leave, and they haul off what they take out.
Call (316) 263-0711 and tell us what's going on in your house: which rooms are cold or hot, where the draft is, what you want done.

sections.heading: When a Window Stops Doing Its Job
body: Windows wear out in ways you can feel before you can see them. The curtains move with the window shut. The glass is cold to the touch in January and hot in July.

Fog between the panes means the seal around the glass has failed and the air space has filled with moisture. A sash that sticks or won't stay up means the parts that carry it have worn or the frame has shifted.
Street noise coming straight through is the same story. Every one of these is a window that has stopped sealing, and you are heating and cooling the outdoors through it.

sections.heading: Rule Out the Rest of the House First
body: A drafty room is not always a drafty window. Air leaking in through an empty attic, a bare floor or a gap in a wall can feel just like a window problem.
New windows will not fix a room that is cold because there's nothing in the wall behind it. That's a job for [insulation](/insulation-wichita-ks/), and insulation is most of what we do.

So when we come out, we can tell you whether the windows are what's costing you, whether the house is, or whether it's both. If your windows are the problem, replace them. If they're not, we'll say so.

sections.heading: What the Estimate Is For
body: Replacing windows is a big decision, and the estimate is where you make it. You should leave knowing your options, what we can do for you and how long it will take.
That's all an estimate should be. It's a conversation about your house, and you shouldn't have to sign the same day.

sections.quote: I had three different companies come out for estimates, and all of them told me 14 to 18 weeks. Two of the companies told me if I didn't say yes that day they will go up 20% the next day. Heath with New Windows For America was the last company that came out for my estimate, and I'm so glad he did. He went over all my options, what he could do for me, and how long it would take. … I originally was told 14 to 18 weeks (same as the other companies), but they came in 7 weeks! … His crew came out the next week and had them done in one day by a very professional crew!
sections.name: Deric C.

sections.heading: Made to Order, Installed in a Day
body: Replacement windows are built to the size of your openings. That's why there is a wait between the estimate and the day the crew shows up, and it's the part of the job people don't expect.
The install itself doesn't take long. A crew can put in a whole house of windows in a day, as the review above shows.
When the windows arrive, our crew installs them, and the date you were given is a date you can plan around.

sections.quote: Service was great. My windows showed up on time like the salesperson said they would. I love the look of the product. Good quality. I would definitely use this company again.

sections.heading: Comparing Window Quotes
body: If you're getting more than one estimate, compare the same things on each. Ask how many windows are in the quote, how long until they're installed, and what the price covers.
Ask whether the install is part of the price, and who does it: the company's own crew or someone hired for the job. A low number means little if the install date is five months out.
And if anyone tells you the price goes up tomorrow unless you sign today, you can take that as a reason to slow down. A window is something you'll look at every day for years.

sections.heading: Why Vinyl
body: We replace windows with vinyl windows. Vinyl frames don't rot, don't need painting and don't swell shut in the humid months the way an old wood frame can.

A vinyl window has a sealed glass unit and weatherstripping that presses against the sash, so it closes tight and stays closed. In a house that's lost its seals, you can feel that on the first cold day.

items.q: How long until my windows are installed?
items.a: Plan on weeks between the estimate and install day, because the windows are built to order. In the review above, other companies quoted 14 to 18 weeks and ours came in at 7. The install is a day.

items.q: Should I do windows or insulation first?
items.a: If a window is fogged, broken or hard to open, replace it. If your windows are fine and a room is still hot or cold, the attic or floor is the likelier cause, and we do that work too.

items.q: Do you do anything besides windows?
items.a: Yes. Insulation is most of our work, and we also do air sealing, furnaces and air conditioners, siding, roofing and remodeling.

sections.heading: Where Your House Loses Its Comfort
body: In July, the attic is the hottest place in the house, and that heat works its way down into the rooms below. In January, the cold comes up through the floor and the warmth you paid for goes out through the ceiling.
Insulation slows that movement. A house with little or none works against its own furnace and air conditioner all year.

You usually notice it before you understand it: a bedroom that never gets right, a floor you won't walk on barefoot, a utility bill that doesn't match the size of the house. Those often point to insulation before they point to windows.

sections.heading: Attics
body: The attic is where a house gains the most heat in summer and loses the most in winter, so it's the first place to look.
A lot of old attics have thin insulation or none at all.
Before the attic insulation goes in, our crews flag the electrical junction boxes, so the boxes can be found again later and don't get buried.
Some older houses have no way into the attic at all. When that happens, we build an access panel so the crew can get in.

sections.heading: Floors and Crawl Spaces
body: If your floors are cold, look underneath. A house over a crawl space often has bare joists with nothing between your feet and the ground, and the pipes run through that same cold air.

Our crews insulate under the floors and lay a vapor barrier on the ground in the crawl space. They wrap exposed pipes and seal duct work where it meets the floor registers. They also seal the gaps where plumbing comes through, like under a sink.

sections.quote: I am part of a grant project, the crew that was sent to put in weatherization, insulate attic and crawl space, the crew, Zach, Damion and Shorty were amazing!! It was during the bitter cold snap and they just kept working till everything was completed.

sections.heading: Walls
body: Walls are the hardest part of an old house to improve, because you can't see inside them. In an older Wichita house, an exterior wall can have little or no insulation in it.
We insulate exterior walls too, and we'll seal air leaks in the attic on the same visit.

sections.heading: Mobile Homes
body: A mobile home loses much of its heat through the underside. The belly is thin, and the wind gets under it.
We wrap the underside and install insulation behind the wrap. That keeps the cold and the wind from pulling heat out of the floor.

sections.quote: They showed up on time! They were very professional. … They wrapped the underside of our mobile home and installed insulation behind the wrap.

sections.heading: The Weatherization Program
body: A lot of our insulation work happens through the weatherization program run by the South Central Kansas Economic Development District (SCKEDD). We work under that program.

You apply to the program to see if you qualify. The program decides who qualifies and when your home comes up, and the wait can be long. When your home comes up, our crews do the insulation, the air sealing and the other weatherization work.
If you're not sure whether you're in the program, or you want to know where to start, call us.

sections.heading: How a Job Goes
body: Before the work begins, the crew tells you what they're going to do. You aren't left guessing what's going on in your attic or under your floor.
Many insulation jobs are finished in a day. A whole-house job with an attic, a crawl space and air sealing can bring in more than one crew.
When they leave, the work area is clean and the old material is gone.

sections.quote: The supervisor explained everything they were going to do before they started working. I figured they would take all day but they had the job done in no time.
